part: XVI. The Standard Library in Depth

chapters.c: Math, Number and BigInt — Worked Examples

p: Math is a namespace of static functions, never a constructor; Math() throws a TypeError. It works entirely on IEEE-754 doubles, so every result is subject to binary floating point. Math.round rounds half toward positive infinity, which means Math.round(-0.5) is -0 and Math.round(2.5) is 3 while Math.round(-2.5) is -2 — not the symmetric behaviour most people expect. When you need half-away-from-zero rounding, use Math.sign(n) * Math.round(Math.abs(n)). When you need banker's rounding or decimal precision, do not use Math at all; scale to integers or use Intl.NumberFormat.

The integer helpers are the ones worth memorising. Math.trunc drops the fraction (Math.trunc(-2.7) is -2), Math.floor goes down and Math.ceil goes up regardless of sign. Math.sign returns -1, 0, 1, -0 or NaN, so it is safe to use as a multiplier. Math.abs(-0) is 0 but Math.abs is not a way to normalise negative zero — Object.is(x, -0) is the only reliable test, and 1 / -0 is -Infinity. Math.min() with no arguments returns Infinity and Math.max() returns -Infinity, which is why reduce over an empty array with Math.max as the reducer throws a cannot-convert-Infinity-to-number style surprise in unrelated code.

Math.hypot(a, b) avoids the overflow that Math.sqrt(a*a + b*b) suffers when a or b is near Number.MAX_VALUE, because the intermediate squares would overflow to Infinity. Math.fround rounds to the nearest 32-bit float and is useful when you want to know exactly what a Float32Array will store. Math.clz32 counts leading zero bits of a 32-bit integer and is the fastest way to build a bit-length function. Math.imul does a true 32-bit integer multiply, and it is the standard trick behind fast 32-bit hashing such as Math.imul(h, 31) + c.

Randomness deserves care. Math.random returns a double in [0, 1) with roughly 53 bits of state, is not cryptographically secure, and must never be used for tokens, password resets or anything an attacker benefits from guessing. For integers in a range, Math.floor(Math.random() * n) is slightly biased for large n because the double's range is not an exact multiple of n. Use crypto.getRandomValues with rejection sampling for anything unbiased or security-sensitive. To shuffle an array correctly, iterate from the end and swap with a random index at or below the current one — the Fisher-Yates algorithm — because the common sort with a random comparator is both biased and slow.

Every Math function returns NaN when a required argument is not a number, and NaN propagates through the whole calculation. That makes NaN the natural sentinel for a failed numeric conversion, but it also means a single bad row in a data set silently poisons an aggregate. Validate at the boundary with Number.isFinite and treat NaN as a data error rather than letting it spread. Also note that Math functions coerce their arguments, so Math.max(null, 1) returns 1 while Math.max(undefined, 1) returns NaN — another reason to convert explicitly before you compute.

Number is both the primitive wrapper and the holder of the numeric constants. Number.EPSILON is about 2.220446049250313e-16, the gap between 1 and the next representable double; the robust way to compare floats is Math.abs(a - b) <= Number.EPSILON * Math.max(1, Math.abs(a), Math.abs(b)). Never write a === b for computed floats. Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER is 9007199254740991 (2^53 - 1) and anything beyond it can no longer represent consecutive integers, so two distinct large IDs can compare equal. Use BigInt or a string for identifiers beyond that boundary.

The static predicates are all safer than their global cousins. Number.isNaN only returns true for the actual NaN value, whereas the global isNaN coerces first and happily reports that the string "abc" is NaN. Number.isFinite rejects strings, while global isFinite('12') is true. Number.isInteger(1.0) is true because 1.0 and 1 are the same double. Number.isSafeInteger additionally checks the 2^53 bound. Number.parseInt and Number.parseFloat exist so that linting rules can ban the globals, but their behaviour is identical: parseInt stops at the first invalid character, so parseInt('12px') is 12 while Number('12px') is NaN.

The Number() constructor is stricter and often more correct for user input: Number('') is 0 and Number('  ') is 0, but Number('12px') is NaN and Number(null) is 0 while Number(undefined) is NaN. That inconsistency — empty string and null both becoming zero — is a classic source of bugs in forms. Whitelist what you accept: reject when the trimmed value is empty, then convert, then check Number.isFinite. For hex or binary prefixes, Number('0x1f') is 31 and Number('0b101') is 5, but the bases are not available in the two-argument form; use parseInt(text, 16) with an explicit radix, because omitting the radix on older engines could produce octal.

Formatting is where most hand-rolled code goes wrong. toFixed rounds half-up in most cases but is exact only for values the double can represent, so (1.005).toFixed(2) is '1.00' because 1.005 is actually stored marginally below 1.005. toPrecision keeps significant digits, toExponential forces exponential notation. String(x) and x.toString() give the shortest representation that round-trips exactly, which is why String(0.1 + 0.2) is '0.30000000000000004'. For display, prefer Intl.NumberFormat: new Intl.NumberFormat('de-DE', { style: 'currency', currency: 'EUR' }).format(1234.5) produces '1.234,50 €' with correct grouping and symbol placement for the locale.

Binary, hex and exponent forms all lose information you may care about. (255).toString(16) is 'ff' and (255).toString(2) is '11111111'. Number.prototype.toString accepts a radix from 2 to 36 and throws a RangeError outside that range. BigInt literal suffixes, separators such as 1_000_000, and the octal 0o and binary 0b prefixes all improve readability without changing the value. Be careful with the separator rules: they may appear only between digits, so 1_000 is valid but 1__000 and 0x_1f are syntax errors, and a leading zero is not allowed before a separator.

BigInt represents arbitrary-precision integers and is written with an n suffix or the BigInt() function: 9007199254740993n, 0x1fn, 0b1010n. typeof 1n is 'bigint', which is a sixth primitive type, not an object. BigInt values are exact and can grow arbitrarily large, at the cost of being slower than doubles and, crucially, of not being mixable with Number. The expression 1n + 1 throws a TypeError: Cannot mix BigInt and other types. That restriction is deliberate — it prevents silent precision loss — and it means every arithmetic boundary must be converted explicitly in one direction.

Division truncates toward zero: 7n / 2n is 3n, and -7n / 2n is -3n. The remainder operator follows the sign of the dividend, so -7n % 2n is -1n. There is no fractional BigInt and BigInt(1.5) throws a RangeError. Comparisons across types work: 1n === 1 is false because the types differ, but 1n == 1 is true and 1n < 2 is true, because relational operators compare mathematically. Sorting an array of mixed Number and BigInt therefore works with the default comparator, while Set and Map treat 1 and 1n as different keys since SameValueZero includes the type.

JSON is the biggest practical obstacle. JSON.stringify throws a TypeError on BigInt, so any object graph containing one cannot be serialised. The usual fix is a replacer that converts to a string: JSON.stringify(value, (_key, v) => (typeof v === 'bigint' ? v.toString() : v)). On the way back you must decide the reverse mapping yourself, because the string '42' is indistinguishable from a genuine string. If you control the schema, tag big integers explicitly or store them as strings from the start. The structuredClone function does support BigInt natively, so cloning in memory is fine.

Bitwise operators on BigInt are unlimited-width: 1n << 64n is a full 65-bit value, whereas the Number version wraps at 32 bits and 1 << 64 evaluates to 1 because the shift count is taken modulo 32. That difference makes BigInt the right type for hashing, bit masks, cryptography primitives and any protocol field wider than 32 bits. Math functions do not accept BigInt at all, so you need a BigInt-safe minimum, power and absolute value of your own. Exponentiation is built in: 2n ** 64n is exact, and exponentiation by squaring in user code is unnecessary.

Performance is easy to get wrong. Small BigInts are fast in modern engines, but every operation allocates a new heap object, so tight loops over millions of small values can be dramatically slower than using Number. Convert to Number at the edges when the values are known to fit in 2^53, do the heavy arithmetic in BigInt only where exactness matters, and convert back. Above roughly a few thousand bits, the cost of multiplication dominates and schoolbook algorithms are replaced by Karatsuba internally, but the constant factor still dwarfs Number arithmetic.

Practical uses are narrower than the hype suggests. BigInt is the correct type for database identifiers that exceed 2^53, for nanosecond timestamps (Date.now() * 1_000_000n), for cryptographic nonces, and for exact factorial or combinatorics output. It is the wrong type for money if the currency has fractional units — scale to integer cents instead and divide only for display, or use a decimal library. It is also the wrong type for a loop counter you only compare against a length, because the mixed-type comparison rules force conversions on every iteration.

chapters.c: Strings, Text and Unicode in Practice

p: Strings are immutable and every transforming method returns a new string. Methods that search — indexOf, lastIndexOf, includes, startsWith, endsWith — return either a boolean or a position, never a match object. indexOf returns -1 on failure, so a check of if (str.indexOf(x)) is wrong because position 0 is falsy; use includes or compare against -1 explicitly. startsWith and endsWith accept an optional position argument, and endsWith with an explicit length is the reliable way to test a suffix of a slice without allocating one.

The position-based methods are also the allocation-free ones. slice(start, end) accepts negative indices and clamps out-of-range values, returning the empty string instead of throwing. substring swaps its arguments when start is greater than end and treats negatives as zero, which makes it subtly different from slice. substr, the legacy method that takes a length rather than an end index, is deprecated and should not appear in new code. Choosing slice everywhere removes an entire category of off-by-one and sign bugs.

Case conversion is locale-dependent and the default methods are not locale-aware. toUpperCase applies simple case mapping, so the German sharp s 'ß' becomes 'SS' (a length change) and the Turkish dotless i does not behave as a Turkish reader expects. For display and comparison of human text, use toLocaleLowerCase and toLocaleUpperCase with a locale tag. Never use case folding for security decisions: normalising an identifier with toLowerCase is not a substitute for comparing canonical forms, and the Unicode standard does not guarantee that case-insensitive equality is stable across versions.

Padding, repeating and trimming round out the everyday set. padStart and padEnd take a target length and an optional fill string, and they truncate the fill if it would overshoot — so time.padStart(5, '0') on '42' gives '0042'. repeat(n) throws a RangeError for a negative count and can exhaust memory for a huge count, so validate before calling it. trim removes whitespace by the Unicode WhiteSpace and LineTerminator definitions, which includes the non-breaking space and the byte order mark but not every invisible formatting character; zero-width characters survive trim and must be stripped explicitly when normalising user input.

Replacing and splitting deserve their own warning. String.prototype.replace with a string pattern replaces only the first occurrence, which contradicts most people's intuition; use replaceAll or a global regular expression for every occurrence. The replacement string interprets dollar sequences — $$ for a literal dollar, $& for the match, $1 for a capture group — so user-supplied replacement text must be escaped or, better, passed as a function. split with an empty string splits into UTF-16 code units rather than characters, which breaks any astral character; use Array.from(str) or the spread operator when you want code points, and split(//u) only when the regular expression has the unicode flag.

JavaScript strings are sequences of UTF-16 code units, and .length counts code units, not characters. A character outside the Basic Multilingual Plane needs a surrogate pair, so '😀'.length is 2 and text.length is not a character count. codePointAt(0) correctly returns 128512 for that string while charCodeAt(0) returns the high surrogate 55357. To iterate real code points, use the string iterator: for (const ch of text) or [...text], both of which yield whole code points. Array.from(text) does the same and gives you an array you can index.

Reading positions is the awkward part, because indexOf and slice still work in code units. If you need to map between a code-unit offset and a code-point index, iterate and accumulate. For grapheme-aware work, use Intl.Segmenter with granularity grapheme: the family emoji '👨‍👩‍👧‍👦' is eleven UTF-16 code units, seven code points and exactly one grapheme, because the four person emoji are joined by zero-width joiners. A text field that counts text.length will report eleven characters for a single visible symbol. The same segmenter with granularity word or sentence gives you linguistic tokenisation that respects the locale and is far better than splitting on spaces.

Normalisation is essential before comparing or storing text. Unicode allows the letter e with an acute accent to be encoded as a single code point or as e followed by a combining accent, and the two strings are visually identical but not equal. str.normalize('NFC') composes to the short form and is the right default for storage and comparison; 'NFD' decomposes and NFD is what you want when you strip diacritics, because you can then remove the combining marks with a regular expression using the Mark category. Casefold-plus-normalise is the standard recipe for a case-insensitive equality test that is closer to correct than toLowerCase alone.

Emoji introduce their own rules. A base emoji plus a skin-tone modifier is two code points and one grapheme; a flag is a pair of regional indicators; a keycap is a digit plus a variation selector plus an enclosing keycap. Counting these with .length produces nonsense. Also remember that emoji presentation is font-dependent, so a short string can render at an unexpected width and break fixed-width layouts. When you truncate text for display, truncate on grapheme boundaries using the segmenter and append an ellipsis, never by slicing at an arbitrary code-unit index, which can split a surrogate pair and produce a replacement character.

Escaping is where Unicode meets security. Lone surrogates are valid in a JavaScript string but are not valid UTF-8, so encoding such a string with the standard TextEncoder replaces the surrogate with U+FFFD, which silently corrupts data. JSON.stringify will happily emit a lone surrogate as an escape and the receiving system may then reject the payload. Unicode tag characters and bidirectional overrides can reorder displayed text so that code that looks benign reads differently to a compiler or a reviewer — the classic Trojan Source attack. Strip or reject bidi control characters and unassigned code points from identifiers and from anything that will be displayed as code.

Regular expressions gain three important features from the unicode flag. Without u, '.' matches one code unit and a pattern can match half a surrogate pair. With u, code points are treated atomically and escapes such as \u{1F600} work. The v flag, the successor to u, adds set operations in character classes: [\p{Script=Greek}--\p{Letter}] subtracts, [[a-z]&&[^aeiou]] intersects, and the intersection operator also supports nesting. Property escapes such as \p{Letter}, \p{Number} and \p{Script=Han} require u or v and are the only portable way to ask for a Unicode category rather than listing ranges by hand.

Slug generation has to survive real input. The recipe is: normalise to NFD, strip combining marks, lowercase with the locale, replace every run of characters outside the allowed set with a single hyphen, then trim leading and trailing hyphens. Anchor the pattern with the unicode flag so an astral character counts once. Never use a global replace with a per-character pattern without collapsing, or a title with several consecutive punctuation marks produces a run of hyphens. Store the original text alongside the slug, because slugs are lossy and cannot be reversed.

Title casing is not uppercasing the first letter of every word. Article and preposition rules vary by style guide, hyphenated compounds have their own rules, and all-caps acronyms must be preserved. A practical approach splits on word boundaries with a regular expression that keeps the separators, applies an exception list, and rejoins. Resist the temptation to build a general solution: title case is a house style, so expose the exception list as configuration and keep the algorithm small. The same reasoning applies to sorting names, where family-name-first conventions vary by locale and cannot be inferred from the string alone.

Sanitising user text for display is a rendering concern, not a string concern. Escaping happens at the moment of insertion into HTML, attribute, URL or JavaScript context, and the rules differ for each. Doing it earlier, when storing, is a mistake because the same value may later be used in several contexts. Build small named helpers such as escapeHtml, escapeAttribute, encodeURIComponentForQuery and use them at the boundary. Never attempt to sanitise by removing angle brackets with a regular expression: HTML is not a regular language and the classic bypasses exploit exactly that assumption.

Deduplicating and normalising lists of strings is a common task with a subtle correctness requirement. If you compare with toLowerCase you will merge strings that differ only in case, which may or may not be what you want for identifiers. For display values, normalise with NFC and compare case-folded; for identifiers, compare exactly. Use a Set for the dedupe but keep the first occurrence's spelling, so the output preserves the author's formatting rather than whichever variant happened to sort first. Sorting the result afterwards with Intl.Collator gives a stable, human-ordered list.

Wrapping and truncating for display must account for the fact that monospace assumptions break for CJK text, where a character occupies two columns. Intl.Segmenter with granularity grapheme gives you the units, and a width function that counts East Asian wide and fullwidth characters as two gives the columns. Combining marks, zero-width joiners and variation selectors occupy zero columns. A correct width function is a small table of ranges plus the segmenter, and it is worth writing once because every naive implementation eventually ships a broken terminal table.

Finally, never build SQL, shell commands, or file paths by concatenating strings. Parameterised queries, argument arrays passed to an exec function, and path.join with basename validation are the only safe forms. String manipulation is not a security boundary. Reserve templating for messages and documents you fully control, and treat every value that came from a user, a network response or a filename as hostile until it has been validated against an explicit allow-list of shape and length.

A Date is a single number: milliseconds since the Unix epoch, 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z. Everything else is projected through a time zone. The value can be at most 8.64e15, roughly plus or minus 100 million days, and anything outside that range is an invalid date whose getTime() is NaN. Critically, an invalid date does not throw; it silently propagates NaN through every getter and through arithmetic, so a parse failure can travel a long way before surfacing as 'Invalid Date' in the UI. Always check Number.isNaN(date.getTime()) immediately after constructing from untrusted input.

The constructor has three entirely different meanings depending on argument shape. new Date(2024, 0, 1) treats the numbers as local components with a zero-based month, so month 0 is January. new Date('2024-01-01') is parsed as UTC because the date-only form has no time zone and the specification says date-only strings are UTC, while new Date('2024-01-01T00:00') is parsed as local time. That asymmetry means the same literal can produce two different instants on two machines. The only unambiguous strings are full ISO 8601 with an explicit offset or Z, and even then engines historically disagreed about non-ISO formats such as '01/02/2024'. Parse explicitly.

Months are zero-based and days of the month are not, so getMonth returns 0 to 11 while getDate returns 1 to 31. Engines normalise overflow rather than throwing: new Date(2024, 12, 1) is January 2025, and new Date(2024, 1, 30) is March 1. That normalisation is genuinely useful — the last day of a month is new Date(year, month + 1, 0) — but it also hides typos. getDay returns the weekday from 0 for Sunday while getUTCDay does the same in UTC. The local getters and the UTC getters are easy to mix, and mixing them is the single most common source of off-by-one-day bugs.

getTimezoneOffset returns the difference in minutes between UTC and local time, with the sign inverted relative to the usual convention: for a time zone ahead of UTC it is negative. The value depends on the instant, because of daylight saving, so it must be queried per date rather than cached. DST transitions create local times that do not exist (the spring forward hour) and local times that occur twice (the autumn overlap). Constructing a date inside a skipped hour yields a shifted instant, and there is no way to represent the ambiguity of the repeated hour at all in a Date. This is the fundamental reason not to store future local wall-clock times as Date values.

Arithmetic on Dates goes through the numeric value. date2 - date1 is a difference in milliseconds, and adding 86_400_000 adds exactly one day of absolute time, which is one hour short or long across a DST boundary. For calendar arithmetic, set components instead: compute the target year, month and day and let the constructor normalise. getTime() and valueOf() are interchangeable and make comparison with < and > work directly. Never use the equality operators on Date objects: two distinct objects holding the same instant are not === because they are different references; compare getTime() values.

Copying and cloning must be explicit. Dates are mutable and passed by reference, so a function that receives a date and calls setHours mutates the caller's object. Clone with new Date(original) or new Date(original.getTime()). The structuredClone algorithm preserves Dates, so structuredClone(date) is a correct deep copy, unlike JSON round-tripping, which turns a Date into an ISO string and loses the type. Date.parse is the static twin of the string constructor and returns NaN for invalid input, while Date.UTC returns a numeric timestamp from UTC components and is the right building block when you want an instant rather than a local component date.

Store instants in UTC, present them in the user's zone, and keep the zone as data. The IANA database names such as Europe/Berlin and America/New_York are the ones to persist, not fixed offsets, because offsets change with daylight saving and with political decisions. An offset of +02:00 tells you where a place was at one instant; a zone name tells you where a place has been and will be. The Intl APIs accept a timeZone option with an IANA name, and Intl.DateTimeFormat().resolvedOptions().timeZone reports the runtime's current zone.

Intl.DateTimeFormat is the correct formatting tool and replaces hand-written month arrays. new Intl.DateTimeFormat('en-GB', { dateStyle: 'long' }).format(date) produces a fully localised long date, and options such as timeZone, hour12 and calendar are all honoured. Formatters are expensive to construct because they perform locale resolution, so build one per locale and reuse it; creating one inside a render loop is a measurable performance problem. formatToParts gives you the pieces plus their types, which is how you build a custom layout without guessing where the fields sit in a locale.

Relative formatting is built in too. Intl.RelativeTimeFormat('en', { numeric: 'auto' }).format(-1, 'day') yields 'yesterday' rather than '1 day ago', and the difference between the plural and the past tense is handled by the locale data instead of a hard-coded table. The format method takes a signed number and a unit, so you convert a millisecond difference into the largest sensible unit yourself. Intl.ListFormat handles the and/or joining of lists, and Intl.DisplayNames resolves language, region and currency codes to readable names, all from the same locale data.

Parsing localised dates back is deliberately hard, and for good reason. There is no locale-aware date parser in the standard library. Accept ISO 8601 or a small set of explicitly configured patterns, validate the components, and construct with the numeric constructor so no implicit zone interpretation can happen. For a date picker, keep the value as an ISO string in state and format only for display. When a user types a date, use a library or a constrained input rather than trying to invert Intl.DateTimeFormat output.

Duration arithmetic needs a policy. Adding a month to January 31 has no single right answer: some systems clamp to February 28 or 29, others roll over to March 3. Decide once and document it, because the two choices produce different results in billing, subscription and reporting code. Adding a year to February 29 behaves the same way. Adding a fixed number of milliseconds is a different operation entirely from adding a calendar day, and mixing them is how reports end up an hour off after a daylight saving change.

For anything stored, prefer the ISO 8601 string with an offset, which is sortable, unambiguous and human readable, or an integer millisecond timestamp, which is compact and exact. Avoid storing a formatted local string, which is neither sortable nor zone-independent, and avoid storing an offset alone for future dates. When you must preserve the user's intended wall-clock time — a daily reminder at 09:00 — store the local time plus the zone name and resolve it at the moment of use, so the reminder stays at 09:00 local rather than drifting an hour twice a year.

Temporal is the long-planned replacement for Date and it splits the single conflated type into distinct ones, which is the whole point. Temporal.Instant is an exact point on the timeline with nanosecond precision and no zone. Temporal.ZonedDateTime is an instant plus a time zone, and it is the type that can represent ambiguous and skipped local times correctly. Temporal.PlainDate, PlainTime, PlainDateTime and PlainYearMonth are wall-clock values with no instant attached. Temporal.Duration is a length of time expressed in calendar units. Because the types are separate, the compiler and the reviewer can see whether a value is an instant or a wall clock.

The names make the intent explicit and remove the zero-based month trap: PlainDate.from({ year: 2024, month: 1, day: 31 }) is the thirty-first of January. Arithmetic uses add and subtract with a duration object: date.add({ months: 1 }) clamps to the last valid day by default, and the overflow option can be set to 'reject' to throw instead. The until and since methods produce a Duration between two values, with a largestUnit option that controls whether the answer is expressed in days or split into months and days. That decision is exactly the policy question Date could not express.

ZonedDateTime resolves the daylight saving problems that Date cannot. When a local time is skipped, the disambiguation option chooses 'compatible', 'earlier', 'later' or 'reject'. When a local time repeats, 'compatible' picks the earlier offset, which is the usual convention. Times are stored as the instant plus the zone, so an addition of one day and an addition of twenty-four hours are different operations and both are expressible. That distinction is the reason to adopt Temporal for scheduling, calendars and reminders rather than continuing to compute with milliseconds.

Support and adoption are the practical concern. Temporal reached Stage 3 and has shipped in some engines; in others it is available through a polyfill. Import the polyfill once at the application entry point and feature-detect rather than branching everywhere: if (typeof Temporal === 'undefined') install the polyfill, then use the global. Do not add the polyfill to a library's own bundle, because a duplicate polyfill can shadow a native implementation and each copy has its own objects that fail instanceof checks against the other.

Convert at the boundaries and keep one representation internally. Date.prototype.toTemporalInstant converts an old Date to an Instant, and Instant.prototype.toZonedDateTimeISO produces a ZonedDateTime. When you must interoperate with an API that speaks milliseconds, convert once at the edge with epochMilliseconds. Because Temporal objects are immutable, adding or rounding returns a new value, so there is no aliasing hazard and no need to clone before mutating — the opposite of the Date situation and one of the main reasons the new API exists.

Rounding and comparison are explicit. Temporal.Duration.prototype.round takes a smallestUnit and a roundingMode such as 'halfExpand' or 'trunc', which removes the ambiguity of the hand-written divide-and-floor code that most applications have somewhere. Comparison operators do not work on Temporal objects directly, so use Temporal.PlainDate.compare or ZonedDateTime.compare, which return the usual negative, zero and positive values and therefore drop straight into a sort comparator. That explicitness is the trade-off the API makes for correctness, and it is worth the extra characters.

Array.prototype.sort compares by UTF-16 code unit order, which puts every uppercase letter before every lowercase letter, sorts accented letters into arbitrary positions and places digits and punctuation according to their code points. For human text that is almost always wrong. Intl.Collator encodes a locale's collation rules, and new Intl.Collator('de').compare('ä', 'z') returns a negative value because German sorts the umlaut near the letter a, whereas the code-unit comparison would place it after z. Use the collator's compare function directly as the sort comparator instead of wrapping it, and reuse the collator instance.

The collator options change the answer in ways the locale alone does not capture. sensitivity controls how much difference matters: 'base' ignores case and accents, 'accent' ignores case, 'case' ignores accents, 'variant' (the default) distinguishes everything. numeric: true makes 'item2' sort before 'item10', which is what people expect for filenames and versioned headings. caseFirst: 'upper' puts uppercase first. Ignore-punctuation and usage: 'search' tune the collator for matching rather than ordering. Because these are construction options rather than call options, you need one collator per distinct combination and should build them at module scope or memoise them by key.

String.prototype.localeCompare is the convenience form and takes a locale and the same options object, but constructing a collator per call is significantly slower in a sort over thousands of items. The rule of thumb is: one comparison, use localeCompare; a loop, build a collator. Be careful that localeCompare's return value is only guaranteed to be negative, zero or positive, not specifically -1, 0 or 1, so never test for equality with -1. Equality with zero is safe and is the correct way to ask whether two strings are equal under a given locale's collation.

Locale negotiation is itself a feature. The Intl constructors accept an array of preferred locales and resolve to the best match using the Lookup or Best Fit algorithm, which is what Intl.getCanonicalLocales and Intl.DateTimeFormat.supportedLocalesOf expose. resolvedOptions() tells you which locale was actually chosen, and you should display that rather than the one you requested, so a user who asked for a fallback sees what they got. Passing an invalid locale tag throws a RangeError, so validate user-supplied tags rather than letting a malformed value crash a formatter built at startup.

Sorting stability matters when you sort by several keys. The specification now requires a stable sort, so sorting by the secondary key first and the primary key second produces the expected grouping. Combining a locale-aware comparator for text with a numeric comparator for scores means the comparator must return a number in every branch; a comparator that returns undefined or a boolean silently produces an implementation-defined order. Write the comparator as an explicit chain of comparisons, each one returning the first non-zero result.

Finally, remember that collation is a property of the locale, not of the text. The same two strings can order differently under two locales and there is no universally correct order. For data that must be ordered identically on a server and a client — cache keys, shards, pagination cursors — use code-unit order and document it, because locale-aware ordering depends on the ICU version and can change between releases. Keep the two orderings separate and name them clearly: a display order for humans and a canonical order for machines.

Intl.NumberFormat replaces every hand-written thousands-separator function. The constructor takes a locale and options, and format takes a number. Key options are style, which is 'decimal', 'percent', 'currency' or 'unit'; currency plus currencyDisplay, which may be 'symbol', 'narrowSymbol', 'code' or 'name'; minimumFractionDigits and maximumFractionDigits; useGrouping; signDisplay, which can force a plus sign or show negative values in parentheses for accounting; and notation, which switches between 'standard', 'scientific', 'engineering' and 'compact'. Compact notation with compactDisplay: 'short' produces localised abbreviations such as 1.2M, and the abbreviation differs per locale rather than being a suffix you append.

Currency formatting places the symbol according to the locale's rules, not the currency's. A euro amount formatted in en-US appears as €1,234.50 with the symbol in front and a dot decimal separator, while the same value in de-DE is 1.234,50 € with the symbol behind. Both are correct for their locale. If you need the currency's own convention regardless of the user's locale, pass the country that uses it as the locale, or use currencyDisplay: 'code' to remove the ambiguity entirely. Never concatenate a symbol with a pre-formatted number.

Percent and unit styles handle the multiplication and the spacing. Style 'percent' multiplies the input by one hundred, so format(0.075) produces 7.5 percent and format(7.5) produces 750 percent; the double-scaling bug where an already-multiplied value is passed is extremely common. Style 'unit' takes a unit identifier from the sanctioned list — 'kilometer-per-hour', 'byte', 'celsius', 'liter' — and produces the correctly spaced and abbreviated form in each locale. unitDisplay chooses the long, short or narrow form.

Precision options are the safe alternative to toFixed. Setting maximumFractionDigits: 2 produces exactly the rounding a display layer wants without the binary representation trap, because the formatter rounds the exact decimal expansion of the double rather than the stored approximation in a way that matches user expectations better than toFixed. minimumFractionDigits forces trailing zeros for money. roundingMode selects halfExpand, halfTrunc, halfEven or one of the directed modes, and halfEven is what you want for statistical and financial aggregation where consistent ties matter.

Parsing localised numbers back into values has no standard API, so treat formatted output as display-only and keep the raw number in state. When you must accept localised input, infer the group and decimal separators from Intl.NumberFormat.formatToParts on a known value such as 1234.5, then strip groups and replace the decimal separator before calling Number. This is more robust than hard-coding a list of separators, and it adapts automatically to the resolved locale. Reject any string that still contains unexpected characters after normalisation.

Performance and caching follow the same rule as other Intl objects: construct formatters once. A formatter is a resolved bundle of locale data, and building one per cell in a table is the classic performance mistake in internationalised applications. For large tables, consider caching by a composite key of locale plus options serialised to a string, and cap the cache so a page that formats in many currencies does not grow it without bound. Above roughly ten thousand rows, format once per distinct value rather than per row when the distinct set is small.

s.t: Plural rules, segmentation and relative time
p: Intl.PluralRules answers the question that hard-coded English pluralisation gets wrong. select(n) returns 'zero', 'one', 'two', 'few', 'many' or 'other' according to the locale's rules, and the categories differ per language: Polish has several distinct plural forms, Japanese collapses to a single form, and Arabic distinguishes all six. The modern approach is the ICU message syntax with a plural branch, or a lookup table keyed by the category returned from select. Never write a ternary that tests whether a count equals one outside English, and never assume a plural category maps to a specific number.

Plural rules also handle ordinals. Constructing with type: 'ordinal' gives the categories used for first, second, third, and the English 'one' category covers 1, 21, 31 while 'two' covers 2, 22 and 'few' covers 3, 23. That is the correct engine behind an English date suffix and it degrades correctly in languages that have no ordinal distinction. The same object with selectRange can express a range such as 'one to three items', which is a category of its own in some languages and cannot be derived by formatting the endpoints separately.

Intl.Segmenter does the word, sentence and grapheme splitting that splitting on spaces cannot do. Chinese, Japanese and Thai have no spaces between words, so a whitespace split produces one giant token; the segmenter uses locale-specific dictionaries. It also returns an isWordLike flag per segment, which filters out punctuation and whitespace and gives you a usable token stream for highlighting, search terms and word counts. The returned segments are a lazy iterable, so materialise it with Array.from when you need random access and keep it lazy when you are streaming.

Grapheme segmentation is the correct basis for a character counter and for truncation. A form field that shows the number of UTF-16 code units will disagree with the number of visible symbols whenever the user types an emoji, an accented letter in decomposed form or a flag. Counting grapheme clusters with the segmenter gives the number a human would count. When enforcing a maximum length, enforce it in graphemes and reject the input rather than truncating silently mid-cluster, which would corrupt the value.

Intl.RelativeTimeFormat, Intl.ListFormat and Intl.DisplayNames complete the set for user-facing prose. Relative time takes a signed amount and a unit and produces the localised phrase, including the tense; ListFormat joins an array with the locale's conjunction or disjunction, handling the final separator and the empty and single-element cases; DisplayNames turns a language tag, region code, currency or script into a readable name in a chosen locale. Together they remove most hand-written string tables from an application, and they update with the runtime's ICU data instead of going stale in your source.

The common thread is to move every locale-dependent decision into Intl and keep the application logic locale-free. Message text still needs a translation layer, but the grammar around the interpolated values — plural categories, connecting words, name of the language being shown, ordering of a formatted list — should come from Intl whenever it can. That division keeps the translation files small and makes it far less likely that a translator is asked to fix a grammar bug that is really a code bug.

btoa and atob convert between a Latin-1 string and base64. The trap is the word Latin-1: btoa throws an InvalidCharacterError on any code point above 255, so btoa('héllo') throws in some environments and btoa('😀') always does. The correct round trip for arbitrary text is to encode to bytes first and then to base64. In a browser that is btoa(String.fromCharCode(...new TextEncoder().encode(text))), and the reverse is new TextDecoder().decode(Uint8Array.from(atob(b64), c => c.charCodeAt(0))). Node has the shorter Buffer.from(text, 'utf8').toString('base64') and Buffer.from(b64, 'base64').toString('utf8').

The spread form of String.fromCharCode has a second trap: it passes every byte as a separate argument, so a megabyte of data blows the argument limit and throws a RangeError about too many arguments. Chunk the input or, better, use the Buffer or TextEncoder paths that never build an argument list. This is a common intermittent failure that only shows up with large payloads, which makes it easy to ship and hard to reproduce.

Hex is the other encoding you meet constantly. A byte array to a hex string is the map-and-pad idiom: [...bytes].map(b => b.toString(16).padStart(2, '0')).join(''), and the reverse is a pair-wise parseInt with radix 16, with validation, because parseInt('zz', 16) returns NaN and a naive loop silently produces a broken array. Hex is case-insensitive on input and conventionally lowercase on output; normalise before comparing digests, since 'AB' and 'ab' are the same value but not the same string.

Binary data in JavaScript is a family of views over one ArrayBuffer. Uint8Array is the general byte array; Int16Array and Float64Array reinterpret the same memory with different widths; DataView gives you explicit endianness control when reading a binary format. Endianness is little-endian on virtually every platform you will run on, but the platform is not guaranteed to be, so a protocol parser must use DataView with an explicit littleEndian flag rather than relying on typed-array views. Also note that TypedArray.prototype.sort sorts numerically while Array.prototype.sort sorts lexicographically, which is a real surprise when you move code between the two.

Base64 has a URL-safe variant that swaps the plus and slash for a hyphen and an underscore and drops the padding. JWT segments, URL parameters and filenames need it, and a standard base64 payload containing a plus will be interpreted as a space if it travels through a query string unescaped. Buffer supports the 'base64url' encoding, and in the browser you translate the two characters yourself. Never assume a base64 string is safe to embed in a URL, an email header or a filename without choosing the right alphabet.

Finally, base64 is not encryption and not compression. It inflates data by about thirty-three percent, so base64-encoding a large binary payload in JSON is a meaningful cost. It is appropriate for small opaque blobs inside a text protocol and for embedding assets in a stylesheet or a document, and inappropriate as an optimisation. If size matters, compress first and then encode, and remember that both steps are reversible transformations with no confidentiality property at all.

The URL constructor parses according to the WHATWG URL standard and normalises as it goes. new URL('/a/b?x=1', 'https://example.com') resolves the relative reference against the base, which is the reliable way to resolve links without writing string joins. It percent-encodes the path using the path-safe set, lowercases the scheme and host, removes the default port and drops a trailing empty fragment. Components are exposed as href, protocol, host, hostname, port, pathname, search, hash, username and password, plus origin which is read-only. Reading a component never fails; assigning an invalid value throws a TypeError.

Percent-encoding is context-dependent and the four global functions are not interchangeable. encodeURI escapes a whole URL and leaves the reserved characters that structure it intact, so it will not protect a query value containing an ampersand or an equals sign. encodeURIComponent escapes a single component and also escapes the reserved set, which is what you want for a parameter value but not for a whole URL. decodeURI and decodeURIComponent are their inverses. Passing a lone surrogate to any of them throws a URIError, so validate before encoding.

URLSearchParams is the correct way to read and write query strings. Construct it from a string, from a URL, from a record or from an array of pairs, then use get, getAll, has, set, append, delete and sort. set replaces every existing value for a key while append adds another, which is exactly the distinction you need for repeated parameters such as tag. Iteration yields the decoded pairs, so you do not decode twice. The class also accepts a full URL string in modern engines and parses just the search portion, which removes the manual split on the question mark.

Do not hand-roll query parsing. Splitting on the ampersand and then on the equals sign breaks on an encoded ampersand inside a value, loses the distinction between a key with an empty value and a key with no value, and mishandles the plus sign, which means space in application/x-www-form-urlencoded but means plus in a raw URL. URLSearchParams handles all of that. The reverse mistake is equally common: taking a URL, slicing off the query, mutating it as text and reattaching, which loses encodeURI's canonicalisation and can produce a URL that the server rejects.

The URLPattern API is the modern router and matcher. It compiles a pattern with named groups over the pathname, search, hash, hostname and protocol, using :name for a single segment, * for a wildcard and {a}? for an optional group. test reports a match and exec returns the captured groups. Building a service worker route, an edge function matcher or a client-side router on URLPattern removes a large amount of bespoke regular expression code and behaves identically to how the platform itself matches URLs. Feature-detect it, since support arrived later than the other URL APIs.

Security rules for URLs are worth stating plainly. Always validate the protocol of a user-supplied URL against an allow-list before using it in a link or a redirect; javascript: and data: URLs are the classic vectors and a substring test for javascript: is trivially bypassed with whitespace or mixed case. Build URLs with the URL class so the parser applies its own canonicalisation, and never concatenate a host from user input into an origin string, because a value containing an at sign or a slash changes the structure of the result. When you only need to display a link, show the parsed hostname rather than the whole string so the user can see where it actually goes.

TextEncoder encodes a string to bytes as UTF-8, and it is a global in browsers and in Node. encoder.encode(text) returns a Uint8Array, while encodeInto writes into a caller-provided array and returns how many code units were read and how many bytes were written. encodeInto is the allocation-free path for large inputs and it is the right tool when you are filling a fixed buffer. Note that encoding replaces a lone surrogate with the three-byte replacement character, so malformed input is silently repaired rather than rejected; if you need to detect it, scan for unpaired surrogates first.

TextDecoder goes the other way and takes a label such as 'utf-8', 'utf-16le', 'latin1' or 'windows-1252'; the label is case-insensitive and normalised, and an unknown label throws a RangeError. The options { fatal: true } make a malformed sequence throw instead of substituting the replacement character, which is what you want when validating a file rather than displaying it. The default is not fatal, so any binary data decoded as UTF-8 will produce a string full of replacement characters rather than an error — a silent corruption that is easy to miss.

The BOM is the classic decoding subtlety. UTF-8 encoded text may begin with the three bytes EF BB BF, and TextDecoder with utf-8 strips a leading BOM by default. Setting ignoreBOM: true keeps it as a visible U+FEFF character, which is occasionally what a parser needs. The same three bytes decode under windows-1252 as ï»¿, which is the signature of a file that was labelled with the wrong encoding. Never guess an encoding from the bytes unless you control the data; require it explicitly or detect it with a dedicated detector.

For streams of text, a byte-oriented decoder is required because a multi-byte character can be split across chunk boundaries. TextDecoderStream wraps a readable stream of Uint8Array chunks and yields strings, holding back an incomplete trailing sequence until the next chunk arrives. A naive TextDecoder().decode(chunk) per chunk corrupts data at every boundary that splits a character, which is a bug that only appears with non-ASCII text and chunk sizes that happen not to align. In Node the same is true of a StringDecoder, and using readAsText on a Blob or calling response.text() is the shortcut that avoids the issue entirely when the whole payload fits in memory.

Reading a file in the browser and in Node look different but share the pipeline. In the browser a File gives you arrayBuffer(), text(), stream() and slice(); text() decodes as UTF-8, and for any other encoding you must take the arrayBuffer and decode with the right label. In Node fs.promises.readFile accepts an encoding or returns a Buffer, and createReadStream paired with a TextDecoderStream is the streaming form. In both cases the important discipline is to know the encoding at the boundary and convert once, rather than letting untyped strings flow through a pipeline.

Finally, choose the serialisation format deliberately. JSON is UTF-8 by specification and cannot represent binary data without an encoding step. CSV needs an explicit encoding and a delimiter convention, and Excel on some platforms assumes a locale-specific one unless a BOM is present. Newline-delimited JSON is the format to reach for when you want streaming and human readability together: each line is an independent value, so you can process a huge file with constant memory and recover from a corrupt line by skipping it. Whatever you pick, validate by round-tripping a value containing an emoji, a combining accent and a literal newline before you ship.
